passages.t: ‘Sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth’
passages.happening:
Psalm 96 has no heading. It opens with a call that keeps widening. “Sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth” (verse 1). Not only Israel, but every land.

The song has a message for the nations. “Declare His glory among the nations, His wonderful deeds among all peoples” (verse 3). The reason: “For all the gods of the nations are idols, but it is the LORD who made the heavens” (verse 5).

Then it calls the families of the earth to come and worship. “Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the nations, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength” (verse 7). They are to “bring an offering and enter His courts” (verse 8). “Worship the LORD in the splendor of His holiness; tremble before Him, all the earth” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Almost all of Psalm 96 appears again in 1 Chronicles 16, in the song sung when David brought the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. The book page notes that that song is made of lines found in Psalms 105, 96 and 106. Scholars differ on which came first, the psalm or the song in Chronicles.

Verse 5 has a pun in Hebrew. The ‘gods’ are elohim. But they are only elilim, a word for worthless things or idols. The two words sound alike. One is a word for God. The other means nothing at all.

In the ancient world each nation had its own gods. A conquering army often carried off the statues of a defeated people's gods. So to tell all the nations that their gods were nothing, and that Israel's God made the sky, was very bold.

Verse 8 would surprise an Israelite. The nations are invited to bring offerings into God's courts. Worship was not meant to stay inside one people forever.
passages.later: Jesus sent his followers to “make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19). In Revelation an angel flies with the gospel “to every nation and tribe and tongue and people”, calling, “Worship the One who made the heavens and the earth and the sea and the springs of waters” (Revelation 14:6-7).
passages.asks:
What is the ‘new song’ in your life? Something God has done that you have not yet thanked him for? Sing it, in words or in music.

Psalm 96 also asks a hard question. What are the ‘worthless things’ that people around you treat as gods: money, power, fame, comfort? Notice that the psalm answers them not with anger but with an invitation: come and worship the one who made the heavens.

passages.t: ‘He is coming to judge the earth’, and the trees sing
passages.happening:
The psalm gives the nations a message to spread. “Declare among the nations: ‘The LORD reigns!’” (verse 10). Because he reigns, the world is firm. “He will judge the peoples with equity” (verse 10). Equity means fairness: the same rule for all.

Then the whole creation joins in. “Let the heavens be glad and the earth rejoice; let the sea resound, and all that fills it” (verse 11). “Let the fields exult, and all that is in them. Then all the trees of the forest will sing for joy” (verse 12).

Why are they glad? The psalm ends by saying that the LORD is coming. “He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in His faithfulness” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
To many people today ‘judgment’ sounds like bad news. To the first hearers it often sounded like good news. In a world where the strong crushed the weak and judges took bribes, the coming of a fair judge meant that wrongs would at last be put right. That is why the trees sing.

Notice that the judging is ‘with equity’ and ‘in His faithfulness’. The judge does not favour one people over another. The psalm gives no nation a head start before him.

The picture of fields and forests singing is poetry, but it says something real. In the Bible the whole creation, not only people, is waiting for God to set things right.
passages.later:
Paul told the people of Athens that God “has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed” (Acts 17:31), and pointed to the resurrection of Jesus.

Paul also wrote that “the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God” (Romans 8:21). Isaiah pictured the trees of the field clapping their hands (Isaiah 55:12).
passages.asks:
Do you think of God's judgment as good news or bad news? Psalm 96 invites you to see it from the side of the poor and the wronged, for whom a fair judge is the best news there is.

And look around you today: the sky, a tree, a field. The psalm says they too are waiting for the LORD. You can join their song.
